text: Unit 3, 3.1. I want to focus today on something that some of you might find unpleasant, but which in fact is very important in the history, and perhaps also the future, of medicine. Does anybody know how medical experts in ancient times treated illnesses? Ancient Egyptians used honey, didn't they? If we had been alive in those days, we might have used honey for treating cuts or wounds, in the same way people today use cream to stop themselves getting infected. I didn't know that. Honey isn't used today in medicine, is it? Well, if you have a sore throat, hot drinks with honey can help. But what I really wanted to talk about was a kind of therapy called Heruto therapy. You don't know what that is, do you? It's some way of treating people, isn't it? Well, yes. It's something that's thought to have started in ancient Egypt. The first recorded use of Heruto therapy was 3,500 years ago, and it involves a small creature. Oh, is it using leeches? That's right. What's a leech? Those black things that live in rivers or lakes that stick onto animals or people and suck their blood. Oh! It wasn't just ancient Egyptian doctors that used leeches. They were commonly used in the Middle East and Europe. In the 17th and 18th centuries, they were so popular that there was a shortage of leeches. In just one year, in 1831, one hospital in Manchester in the UK used 50,000 of these creatures. But in the 20th century, medical science began to think it had no more use for them. I'm not surprised. If I'd been around then, I wouldn't have allowed a doctor to use them on me. Using leeches didn't actually help anybody, did it? As I see it, no. Medieval doctors thought the human body had four different elements. Blood was one of them. If you had all these elements in balance, then you were thought to be healthy. However, when people had a fever, their skin would often get red and hot. Some doctors thought this meant too much blood in the body. So I'm guessing leeches were one method they used to help let some blood out, getting the body back in balance. Correct. But as I hinted at earlier, leech therapy is growing in importance. Why is that? There are several laboratories in the world right now growing leeches for medical use. They're being used to do something that can't be done in other way, aren't they? Yes, but what? It's something to do with grafts. You know what a graft is, don't you? It's when you attach one piece of your body to another. For example, if someone's badly burnt their skin in an accident, you can get healthy skin from another part of their body and attach it to the damaged part to help it recover. That's right. Now, how would leeches help with this? It would be something to do with blood, wouldn't it? I know that sometimes when people have a graft, their bodies reject it. Unfortunately, yes. What often occurs is that the blood starts to get hard in that area of the body. That part of the body can even die. So placing leeches on those parts of the body helps it stay alive? Oh, I see. Because they suck the blood and keep it moving. Exactly. It turns out that what leeches are good at is keeping blood flowing. There's data to show how successful they are. In one study, doctors reported a 78% success rate in 277 different cases. And in 2004, the US government approved leeches for proper scientific use, making them the first ever living medical tool. From my perspective, I can't imagine myself having these little creatures on me. It's quite disgusting, isn't it? As far as I'm concerned, if I had a bad accident, I'd want doctors to do whatever was necessary to help me recover. I think most people would, the same negative reaction to this treatment that I would. In my opinion, there's very little about medicine that's pretty, is there? Yeah, but a living medical tool? To me, that's a bit too unpleasant. Well, it seems to me that until technology can develop something that does the job as well as leeches, perhaps some kind of robot, then this is an interesting and practical solution. Those are some interesting views. Thanks, everyone.
